{{short description|Solution concept in Game Theory}}
{{Infobox equilibrium
|name=Cursed equilibrium
|supersetof=[[Bayesian game#Bayesian Nash equilibrium|Bayesian Nash equilibrium]]

In [[game theory]], a '''cursed equilibrium''' is a [[solution concept]] for [[static game]]s of [[Bayesian game|incomplete information]]. It is a generalization of the usual [[Bayesian game#Bayesian Nash equilibrium|Bayesian Nash equilibrium]], allowing for players to underestimate the connection between other players' equilibrium actions and their types – that is, the [[behavioral bias]] of neglecting the link between what others know and what others do. Intuitively, in a cursed equilibrium players "average away" the information regarding other players' types' mixed strategies.

The solution concept was first introduced by [[Erik Eyster]] and [[Matthew Rabin]] in 2005,<ref name = "eyster2005">{{cite journal |last1=Eyster |first1=Erik |last2=Rabin |first2=Matthew |author2-link=Matthew Rabin |title=Cursed Equilibrium |journal=Econometrica |date=2005 |volume=73 |issue=5 |pages=1623–1672| doi = 10.1111/j.1468-0262.2005.00631.x}}</ref> and has since become a canonical  [[Behavioral game theory|behavioral]] solution concept for Bayesian games in [[behavioral economics]].<ref name = "cohen2022">{{cite arXiv|last1 = Cohen |first1= Shani| last2 = Li|first2= Shengwu |author-link2= Li Shengwu (economist) |date=2022|title= Sequential Cursed Equilibrium|eprint=2212.06025|class=econ.TH}}</ref>

== Preliminaries ==

=== Bayesian games ===

Let <math>I</math> be a finite set of players and for each <math>i \in I</math>, define <math>A_i</math> their finite set of possible actions and <math>T_i</math> as their finite set of possible types; the sets <math>A = \prod_{i \in I} A_i</math> and <math>T = \prod_{i \in I} T_i</math> are the sets of joint action and type profiles, respectively. Each player has a utility function <math>u_i : A \times T \rightarrow \mathbb R</math>, and types are distributed according to a joint probability distribution <math>p \in \Delta T</math>. A finite Bayesian game consists of the data <math>G = ((A_i, T_i, u_i)_{i \in I}, p)</math>.

=== Bayesian Nash equilibrium ===

For each player <math>i \in I</math>, a mixed strategy <math>\sigma_i : T_i \rightarrow \Delta A_i </math> specifies the probability <math>\sigma_i ( a_i |  t_i)</math> of player <math>i</math> playing action <math>a_i \in A_i</math> when their type is <math>t_i \in T_i</math>.

For notational convenience, we also define the projections <math>A_{-i}= \prod_{j \neq i} A_j</math> and <math>T_{-i} = \prod_{j \neq i} T_j</math>, and let <math>\sigma_{-i} : T_{-i} \rightarrow \prod_{j \neq i} \Delta A_j </math> be the joint mixed strategy of players <math>j \neq i</math>, where <math>\sigma_{-i} (a_{-i} | t_{-i})</math> gives the probability that players <math>j \neq i</math> play action profile <math>a_{-i}</math> when they are of type <math>t_{-i}</math>.

'''Definition:''' a '''Bayesian Nash equilibrium''' (BNE) for a finite Bayesian game  <math>G = ((A_i, T_i, u_i)_{i \in I}, p)</math> consists of a strategy profile <math>\sigma = (\sigma_i)_{i \in I}</math> such that, for every <math>i \in I</math>, every <math>t_i \in T_i</math>, and every action <math>a_i^*</math> played with positive probability <math>\sigma_i ( a_i^* |  t_i) > 0</math>, we have

:<math>a_i^* \in \underset{a_i \in A_i}\operatorname{argmax} \sum_{t_{-i} \in T_{-i}} p_i(t_{-i} | t_i) \sum_{a_{-i} \in A_{-i}} \sigma_{-i} (a_{-i} | t_{-i}) u_i (a_i, a_{-i}, t_i, t_{-i}) </math>

where <math>p_i(t_{-i} | t_i) = \frac{p(t_i, t_{-i})}{\sum_{t_{-i} \in T_{-i}} p(t_{i} | t_{-i}) p(t_{-i}) }</math> is player <math>i</math>'s beliefs about other players types <math>t_{-i}</math> given his own type <math>t_i</math>.

== Definition ==
=== Average strategies ===

First, we define the "average strategy of other players", averaged over their types. Formally, for each <math>i \in I</math> and each <math>t_i \in T_i</math>, we define <math>\overline{\sigma}_{-i} : T_i \rightarrow \prod_{j \neq i} \Delta A_{j}</math> by putting

:<math>\overline{\sigma}_{-i} (a_{-i} | t_i)= \sum_{t_{-i} \in T_i} p_i(t_{-i} | t_i) \sigma_{-i} (a_{-i} | t_{-i})</math>

Notice that <math>\overline{\sigma}_{-i} (a_{-i} | t_i)</math> does not depend on <math>t_{-i}</math>. It gives the probability, viewed from the perspective of player <math>i</math> when he is of type <math>t_i</math>, that the other players will play action profile <math>a_{-i}</math> when they follow the mixed strategy <math>\sigma_{-i}</math>. More specifically, the information contained in <math>\overline{\sigma}_{-i}</math> does not allow player <math>i</math> to assess the direct relation between <math>a_{-i}</math> and <math>t_{-i}</math> given by <math>\sigma_{-i} (a_{-i} | t_{-i})</math>.

=== Cursed equilibrium ===

Given a degree of mispercetion <math>\chi \in [0, 1]</math>, we define a
<math>\chi</math>-'''cursed equilibrium'''  for a finite Bayesian game  <math>G = ((A_i, T_i, u_i)_{i \in I}, p)</math> as a strategy profile <math>\sigma = (\sigma_i)_{i \in I}</math> such that, for every <math>i \in I</math>, every <math>t_i \in T_i</math>, we have

:<math>a_i^* \in \underset{a_i \in A_i}\operatorname{argmax} \sum_{t_{-i} \in T_{-i}} p_i(t_{-i} | t_i) \sum_{a_{-i} \in A_{-i}} \left[\chi \overline{\sigma}_{-i} (a_{-i} | t_i) + (1- \chi)\sigma_{-i} (a_{-i} | t_{-i}) \right] u_i (a_i, a_{-i}, t_i, t_{-i}) </math>

for every action <math>a_i^*</math> played with positive probability <math>\sigma_i ( a_i^* |  t_i) > 0</math>.

For <math>\chi = 0</math>, we have the usual BNE. For <math>\chi = 1</math>, the equilibrium is referred to as a ''fully cursed equilibrium'', and the players in it as ''fully cursed''.

== Applications ==

=== Trade with asymmetric information ===

In bilateral trade with two-sided asymmetric information, there are some scenarios where the BNE solution implies that no trade occurs, while there exist <math>\chi</math>-cursed equilibria where both parties choose to trade.<ref name = "eyster2005></ref>

=== Ambiguous political campaigns and cursed voters ===

In an election model where candidates are policy-motivated, candidates who do not reveal their policy preferences would not be elected if voters are completely rational. In a BNE, voters would correctly infer that if a candidate is ambiguous about their policy position, then it's because such a position is unpopular. Therefore, unless a candidate has very extreme – unpopular – positions, they would announce their policy preferences.

If voters are cursed, however, they underestimate the connection between the non-announcement of policy position and the unpopularity of the policy. This leads to both moderate and extreme candidates concealing their policy preferences.<ref name = "szembrot2017">{{cite journal |last1=Szembrot |first1=Nichole |title=Are voters cursed when politicians conceal policy preferences? |journal=Public Choice |date=2017 |volume=173 |issue=1–2 |pages=25–41 |doi=10.1007/s11127-017-0461-9}}</ref>
